meta.title: FROTH-RFC-0019: Chronological Prompt Context and Structured Cycle Trace Memory
meta.author: Codex
meta.classification: Prompt rendering, cache stability, cycle trace structure, and interim query performance.
meta.research: Drafted from live measurements on 2026-03-28 using mix froth.context, explain analyze runs through bin/rpc on froth@igloo, and direct inspection of BotContext, BotContextHTML, Agent, ToolDescription, and the RFC collection.

section.title: Problem
section.p: The current prompt renderer gets several important high-level decisions right. It uses XML-like document boundaries. It keeps the footer separate. It renders one message per part, which is the right instinct for prompt caching. The problem is not that the prompt is informal. The problem is that the most operationally important part of the prompt, the cycle and tool memory, is currently rendered in a way that loses time, structure, and exactness.

Today the recent transcript is built as a raw message tail plus attached analyses and attached cycle traces. That means a tool-heavy bot action appears under the triggering user's message, even when the bot sent Telegram messages during the cycle and even when the human-relevant chronology was interleaved with other events. The transcript shape says "this all belongs inside the user message" when the lived runtime shape is "this was a chronological sequence of messages and agent events."

The other problem is that the recent window is governed by a hard sliding message count. Once the window is full, every new message drops the oldest message from the prefix. That invalidates prompt caching for the entire recent tail even when 99 percent of the tail is unchanged.

The cycle rendering itself also hides exact information in favor of friendly narration. Tool calls prefer prose descriptions over the formal input object. Tool results are aggressively truncated into anonymous text blobs. Status, duration, byte counts, and truncation markers are mostly absent. The current rendering is readable enough for a human skimming the terminal, but it is not a strong memory format for an agent that needs to avoid re-checking the same thing, repeating failed work, or losing the causal structure of a previous investigation.

There is also an immediate operational issue behind the renderer: the hot lookup for latest_head_id is doing a parallel sequential scan over the unified events table. The renderer is therefore paying a large latency cost to reconstruct a representation that still loses important structure after it arrives.

section.title: Current Observations
section.p: Measured on 2026-03-28 against the live Charlie chat through mix froth.context and bin/rpc.
section.code:
clean rendered prompt (system prompt + parts, no logger prelude) 288,300 chars 290,793 bytes ~72K to ~82K tokens by common text heuristics
shape system prompt: 6,165 chars chronicle chapters: 7 parts, 72,778 chars recent messages: 200 parts, 207,166 chars footer: 1 part, 1,567 chars
nontrivial sample in current 200-message window 13 messages selected by --only-messages --no-trivial 10 analysis blocks 3 rendered cycle blocks 15 rendered call blocks 15 rendered return blocks
live query plans latest_head_id current query: ~403ms, parallel seq scan on events latest_head_id narrowed to event = froth.agent.message.appended: ~149ms, bitmap scan on events_event_index load_messages recursive chain: ~0.14ms telegram_cycle_links query for reply_to lookups: ~0.44ms on current table size
section.p: The important distribution is that the unstable recent tail is already the majority of the prompt by bytes. Roughly 72 percent of the prompt is the message tail, 25 percent is chronicle, 2 percent is system prompt, and the footer is negligible. That means cache invalidation in the recent tail dominates runtime cost even though the rest of the prompt is stable.

item.p: Render recent context as a chronological sequence rather than as user messages with buried attached cycle blobs.
Make tool memory formal enough that the bot can reliably see what it already did, with what parameters, with what status, and with what result shape.
Keep XML-like outer structure and footer style; this RFC is not arguing against document tags.
Improve prompt-cache stability by replacing the hard sliding message-count window with anchored or bucketed recent-context boundaries.
Provide an exact inventory of current truncation and omission behavior in the context path.
Identify low-risk interim performance work that improves the current implementation before the larger schema changes land.
This RFC does not argue against XML-like prompt structure. The outer document tags stay.
This RFC does not propose changing the footer into a more formal structure. The current footer is good enough and is not where the memory failure lives.
This RFC does not require that every old cycle remain fully raw forever. Older cycle material is a strong candidate for compaction.
This RFC does not replace the broader layered-memory work in and . It assumes those layers continue to matter.
This RFC does not fully specify the eventual storage migration by itself. The storage direction is already captured in and is referenced here rather than duplicated.

section.title: Thesis
section.p: Froth should keep its layered prompt architecture, but the recent layer should stop being "messages with attached cycle traces" and become a chronological timeline of recent items.

The timeline should be composed of stable document parts and recent timeline parts. Within the recent timeline, chat messages and agent-cycle items should be rendered in chronological order. Tool calls and results should be rendered formally, with exact input and output structure primary and narration secondary. Older raw work should be eligible for compaction on stable time boundaries. The current hard sliding message-count window should be replaced with bucketed or anchored cutoffs so the hot prefix remains cacheable across many messages.

item.p: keep XML-like separation, chapters, and footer
change recent context from a sliding message tail into a chronological recent timeline
replace narration-first cycle rendering with structured cycle memory
stabilize cache boundaries by time buckets or anchored token-budget cutoffs

subsection.title: 1. Temporal inversion
subsection.p: A cycle currently renders inside the triggering user's message entry. In practice that means the prompt shows a user message, then a whole tool transcript, then later bot messages that were actually produced during or after that cycle. The prompt is no longer telling the truth about order.

This matters for agents because temporal order is not cosmetic memory. It is causal memory. When a bot cannot see whether a shell command came before or after a later Telegram reply, it loses the shape of its own action.

subsection.title: 2. Friendly text hides exact inputs
subsection.p: The current renderer prefers narration text over the actual tool input object whenever narration exists. That means the exact parameters disappear precisely in the cases where the tool call was best described. Narration is useful, but exact input should not be sacrificed to obtain it.

This RFC therefore partially reverses the narration-first amendment in for runtime prompt rendering. Narration can remain as a compact human summary field, but it should no longer replace the formal call representation.

subsection.title: 3. Silent truncation obscures failures and detail
subsection.p: Tool results are truncated multiple times and often without an explicit truncation marker. Failure payloads therefore become ambiguous at exactly the moment when the bot most needs to see what went wrong.

subsection.title: 4. Sliding cutoffs destroy cache locality
subsection.p: With a hard message-count window, once the window is full, every new message changes the first recent-message part. Prefix caching therefore stops at the end of the chronicle, and the entire recent tail becomes effectively hot every turn.
The current part structure is almost good enough. The missing idea is to make the cutoff itself stable for a while instead of re-centering it on every single message.

subsection.title: 1. Keep stable layers, but render the recent layer as timeline buckets
subsection.p: The overall prompt should still be layered in the spirit of :

item.p: system prompt
slow-changing memory documents such as chronicle chapters, headlines, summaries, or later hierarchical compressions
recent timeline buckets
footer

subsection.p: The change is that the recent layer should no longer be "exactly the last N messages." Instead it should be emitted as one or more recent buckets with stable boundaries. A four-hour bucket is a plausible starting point. The key property is that the cutoff moves rarely, not every turn.
Within a bucket, new items append. Older buckets remain byte-stable and stay cacheable.

subsection.title: 2. Render chronological recent items, not attached cycle blobs
subsection.p: The recent layer should become a timeline of heterogeneous items:

item.p: Telegram message items
cycle start and stop items
tool call items
tool result items
assistant reply or control items when relevant

subsection.p: Reply linkage should survive as metadata, not as containment. The question "which user message triggered this cycle?" is still useful. It just should not force the entire cycle transcript to live underneath that user message.
The long-term storage shape for this is already described in . This RFC is the prompt-rendering consequence of that storage direction.

subsection.title: 3. Structured tool memory should be exact first and friendly second
subsection.p: Tool calls and results should remain wrapped in XML-like tags, but the interior should become structured and exact. The primary representation for call inputs should be pretty-printed JSON, not prose. JSON is chosen over YAML as the canonical exact form because it is unambiguous, stable under machine production, and already native to the stored tool payloads.
A plausible shape:
subsection.code: <cycle cycle_id="01..." started_at="2026-03-27 21:04:43 UTC" reply_to="64617447424" status="completed"> <tool_call seq="12" tool="run_shell" status="completed" duration_ms="271"> <summary>Looking at what lives in ~/src/superpower</summary> <input format="json"> { "command": "ls ~/src/superpower/" } </input> </tool_call> <tool_result seq="13" tool="run_shell" status="ok" truncated="false" content_type="text/plain" bytes="54"> <output> bun.lock package.json package-lock.json scripts src themes </output> </tool_result> </cycle>
subsection.p: The exact fields can change, but the principles should not:

item.p: status must be explicit
durations and exit or failure signals should be present when known
truncation must be explicit when it occurs
summary is optional and secondary
formal input and output structure is primary

subsection.title: 4. Prefer raw message chronology plus summarized older tool work
subsection.p: Not every cycle trace deserves equal lifetime at full raw fidelity. Recent tool work should stay exact. Older tool work should be eligible for compaction into summaries generated by cheap fast models, especially when the cycle was investigative rather than decisive.
A three-band model is plausible:

item.p: hot band: exact recent raw tool traces
warm band: compacted cycle summaries for older recent buckets
cold band: daily, hourly, weekly, or headline-level memory layers from and

subsection.p: This is especially relevant for tool-heavy days. The work history increasingly dominates the transcript because the robots do more work, not because the family chats more.

section.title: Interim Performance and QoL Work
section.p: The large schema move in should still happen, but there is worthwhile immediate work that improves the current system materially.

subsection.title: 1. Narrow latest_head_id to message.appended
subsection.p: The current query scans all froth.agent.* events with a non-null head_id. On the live node this takes about 403ms and parallel-seq-scans the whole events table.

Restricting the query to event = 'froth.agent.message.appended' drops the measured runtime to about 149ms using the existing events_event_index. That is not good enough, but it is already much better and appears semantically sufficient for current usage because head changes are driven by message appends.

subsection.title: 2. Batch head lookups per context build
subsection.p: The current context builder looks up cycle heads one cycle at a time. Even without a new index, a batched distinct on (cycle_id) lookup over the relevant set of cycle IDs is materially cheaper than many one-cycle queries. A live 3-cycle batch took about 129ms, which is already much better than three separate 149ms narrowed lookups or three separate 403ms current lookups.

subsection.title: 3. Add an expression index for cycle head lookups
subsection.p: The current unified events table has a GIN index on metadata and a btree index on event. The live plan shows that this is not enough for the head lookup query shape.
A strong near-term candidate is a partial expression index like:
subsection.code: create index concurrently events_agent_message_cycle_seq_head_idx on events ( (metadata->>'cycle_id'), (coalesce((metadata->>'seq')::bigint, 0)) desc, (metadata->>'head_id') ) where event = 'froth.agent.message.appended';
subsection.p: This aligns with the actual predicate and sort key instead of hoping that a generic metadata index will help.

subsection.title: 4. Telegram cycle-link indexing is not urgent yet
subsection.p: The current telegram_cycle_links query is doing a sequential scan because the table only has indexes on (bot_id, chat_id) and legacy_inference_session_id. On current live size this query is still sub-millisecond and is not the main bottleneck.
It is still reasonable to add (bot_id, chat_id, reply_to) or (chat_id, reply_to) before the table grows much larger, but this is not the thing currently making mix froth.context feel slow.

section.title: Current Truncation and Omission Inventory
section.p: This section is intentionally exhaustive for the current prompt-context path. It includes selection limits, text truncation, and important silent omissions, because all three affect what the bot can remember.

item.p: Default recent-message window. Charlie's default config uses recent_message_limit: 200. BotContext.limit_recent_rows/2 applies this with Enum.take(rows, -n). This is a hard selection limit. It is silent in the rendered output. The omitted_count field exists in the view model but is currently always zero and never rendered.
CLI message override. mix froth.context --messages N replaces the default limit with another hard count window. This is operator-explicit but still silent in the final prompt rendering.

Nontrivial-only filter. When only_nontrivial is enabled, messages are kept only if they have analyses or cycles. This is intentional and flag-driven, but the output itself does not render a gap marker or omission count.

Analysis snippets. truncate_analyses/1 collapses all whitespace to single spaces, trims, then slices to 150 characters. If the original text was longer, it appends an ellipsis. This is marked, but formatting structure such as headings and paragraphs is flattened before truncation.
Tool-description goals list. ToolDescription.normalize_description/1 keeps only the first 3 goals. This is a hard coded informational limit and is silent.

Tool input encode fallback. If tool input cannot be JSON-encoded, encode_tool_input/1 falls back to inspect(input, limit: 50, printable_limit: 600). This is an inspect-based truncation. It is marked only insofar as Elixir inspect uses abbreviated output.

Tool result inspect fallback. Non-binary, non-list tool results go through inspect(content, limit: 50, printable_limit: 2000). This is inspect-based truncation and only softly marked by inspect syntax.

Per-block fallback in tool-result lists. Unknown blocks inside list results go through inspect(other, limit: 20, printable_limit: 300). Again the truncation is delegated to inspect and is only softly marked.
Tool result hard slice in Agent. extract_trace_entries/1 slices tool result text to 500 characters with String.slice(text, 0, 500). This is a hard coded truncation and is silent.
Tool call fallback in BotContextHTML. If narration is absent, call/1 slices the JSON string to 300 characters. This is a hard coded truncation and is silent.

Cycle return in BotContextHTML. cycle_return/1 slices its text to 500 characters. This is a second hard coded truncation and is silent. In many cases it is redundant because the text was already sliced upstream.
Unknown trace entry fallback. trace_entry/1 falls back to inspect(assigns.entry, limit: 10, printable_limit: 500). This is a fallback-path truncation and is only softly marked by inspect syntax.
send_message tool uses are dropped. extract_trace_entries/1 discards tool_use blocks whose name is send_message. This is not truncation; it is total omission.
"sent" tool results are dropped. Tool results whose normalized text is exactly sent are discarded entirely. Again this is total omission rather than truncation.
Narration replaces exact call input. When narration exists, the renderer shows narration instead of the actual formal input object. This is not text truncation; it is a structural loss of exact data.
Cycle chronology is flattened under the replied-to message. This is not a byte truncation, but it is a major information loss because the timeline no longer reflects temporal order.

section.title: Recommendation
section.p: Adopt a new prompt-context renderer that keeps XML-like document structure and the existing footer, but replaces the recent sliding message tail with chronological recent timeline buckets.
Make tool memory formal: exact inputs, explicit statuses, explicit truncation markers, and typed outputs. Let narration remain as a compact summary field rather than as the primary representation.

Use the storage direction in as the long-term basis for true chronological interleaving. In the meantime, narrow and batch the current head lookups and add a targeted expression index so the existing renderer stops paying a whole-table scan tax for every cycle trace.

section.title: Implementation Status
section.p: As of 2026-07-25, this RFC is partially implemented.

Froth has sequential cycle-item storage, indexed ordered reads, anchored and time-bucketed recent-window algorithms, exact structured tool-call rendering, typed block-backed returns, and blob-backed large outputs.

The principal prompt-context chronology change is not complete. Cycle traces are still attached beneath their triggering Telegram messages rather than interleaved as independent timeline items, and the default Charlie configuration still uses the anchored count fallback rather than the time-and-mass window.
